claims.text: AlCoCrFeNi2.1-type EHEA can possess a fine lamellar FCC/B2 microstructure in the as-cast state.
The material is partially cold-rolled by approximately 5–10% thickness reduction before annealing.
The proposed intervention is a short anneal just below recrystallization onset, exemplified by 600–700 °C for several minutes.
Air cooling or water quenching after the anneal will freeze in a refined lamellar microstructure.
Subcritical annealing after partial cold working will refine lamellar interfaces.
Subcritical annealing will produce partial recovery of dislocation cells and stabilize a refined dual-phase substructure.
During subcritical annealing, dislocations rearrange or annihilate at newly formed or subdivided interfaces.
Dislocation recovery at interfaces mitigates stress concentrations and thereby improves ductility.
Preserved or refined FCC/B2 interfaces provide strengthening.
A fine lamellar FCC/B2 EHEA can exhibit simultaneously high strength and high tensile ductility at room temperature.
The proposed anneal will increase yield or ultimate tensile strength by at least 10–20% relative to the cold-rolled baseline.
The proposed anneal will increase ductility by at least a comparable percentage relative to the cold-rolled baseline.
Partial cold working without subsequent heat treatment leaves the EHEA with reduced elongation while retaining strength from deformation.
The intervention is expected to apply to lamellar FCC/B2 EHEAs used at room to moderate temperatures.
The excellent mechanical properties of the cited as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA can be maintained up to 700 °C.
Excessive annealing temperature or dwell time may cause recrystallization or grain growth that negates strength improvements.
An annealing temperature that is too low may provide insufficient recovery to improve ductility.
The magnitude of improvement depends on alloy composition, annealing temperature, and cold-working level.
The experiment compares identically composed, partially cold-rolled samples annealed at 580–620 °C for 1–30 minutes using room-temperature tensile tests and microstructural characterization.
The hypothesis is falsified if no annealed condition produces statistically significant increases of at least 10% in both strength and ductility relative to the cold-rolled control.
